content: Caesarean section is a frequently performed surgical procedure, but there is no universally accepted standard regarding the techniques or materials used for skin closure. The skin incision can be closed using various methods, including subcuticular sutures placed just beneath the skin layer, interrupted sutures, or staples. A wide range of materials and techniques are employed for this purpose, and it is important to determine which approach yields the best outcomes for patients. The primary objective of this research was to compare the effects of different skin closure techniques and materials on maternal and surgical outcomes following caesarean section. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of January 10, 2012. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different skin closure materials in caesarean sections were selected for analysis. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. A total of 19 trials were identified, of which 11 were included in the review. However, only eight trials provided usable data. Three trials were excluded because they were not RCTs, two were ongoing, one was terminated without available results, one was awaiting classification, and one did not compare skin closure materials but instead focused on suture-to-suture and drain placement. The two most commonly compared methods of skin closure in caesarean sections are non-absorbable staples and absorbable subcutaneous sutures. When comparing these two methods, the incidence of wound infection was found to be similar. Other secondary outcomes, such as wound complications, were also comparable between the two groups in women with Pfannenstiel incisions. However, it is important to note that the effect of staples on outcomes like wound infection and wound complications may vary depending on the type of skin incision, such as Pfannenstiel versus vertical incisions. Non-absorbable staples were associated with a higher risk of skin separation compared to absorbable subcutaneous sutures. This increased risk of skin separation often necessitated reclosure of the wound. However, the definition of skin separation varied across the trials, and in most cases, staples were removed within four days postpartum. In conclusion, there is currently no definitive evidence to recommend one specific method of skin closure over another following caesarean section. Both staples and sutures are associated with similar outcomes in terms of wound infection, pain, and cosmetic results. However, if staples are removed on the third day postpartum, there is an increased likelihood of skin separation and the need for reclosure compared to absorbable sutures. Further research is needed to establish clear guidelines for optimal skin closure techniques in caesarean sections.
